clinicalPearls: The commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults; the large majority arise in the left atrium, typically pedunculated from the margin of the fossa ovalis of the interatrial septum.
The classic clinical triad comprises valvular obstruction, systemic embolisation, and constitutional symptoms.
A low-pitched early-diastolic 'tumour plop' may be audible as the pedunculated mass prolapses into the mitral orifice.
Symptoms and auscultatory findings are often positional, varying with posture as the mobile tumour shifts within the atrium.
Constitutional features (fever, weight loss, arthralgia, anaemia and raised inflammatory markers) are largely driven by tumour interleukin-6 and can mimic infective endocarditis or vasculitis.
The obstructive presentation can closely imitate rheumatic mitral stenosis with exertional breathlessness and pulmonary congestion.
Histological examination of fragments retrieved at embolectomy may first reveal the diagnosis after an embolic event.
Multiple, recurrent, or atypically sited myxomas in a young patient suggest Carney complex, associated with lentigines and endocrine overactivity.
reference.pathophysiology: Cardiac myxoma is a benign neoplasm believed to originate from primitive multipotential mesenchymal cells within the subendocardium, most characteristically at the border of the fossa ovalis, from which it projects into the left atrial cavity as a gelatinous, often pedunculated and mobile mass. Clinical consequences arise through three principal mechanisms. Mechanical obstruction occurs when the tumour intermittently occludes the mitral valve orifice, producing findings that mimic mitral stenosis, with pulmonary venous congestion, positional dyspnoea and syncope. Embolisation of friable tumour fragments or of thrombus formed on the tumour surface disperses material to the systemic circulation, causing cerebral, retinal, visceral or limb ischaemia. Systemic constitutional effects are mediated largely by tumour secretion of interleukin-6, producing fever, weight loss, arthralgia and an acute-phase response. Most cases are sporadic; a minority are familial as part of the autosomal dominant Carney complex, associated with mutations in the PRKAR1A gene and a tendency to multiple and recurrent tumours.
additionalDifferentials: Infective endocarditis with a valvular vegetation
Papillary fibroelastoma and other benign cardiac tumours
Systemic vasculitis or connective tissue disease
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography to define size, attachment site and mobility
Cardiac MRI for tissue characterisation and to help distinguish thrombus or malignant tumour
Cardiac CT where MRI is unavailable or contraindicated
Histopathological examination of the resected mass or of an embolectomy specimen
Full blood count and inflammatory markers (anaemia and a raised acute-phase response)
Coronary angiography before surgery in appropriate patients
Genetic assessment and screening for Carney complex where clinically indicated
redFlags: Acute embolic stroke or other systemic embolisation
Syncope or presyncope suggesting critical intermittent valve obstruction
Imaging features suggesting a malignant tumour (broad-based, infiltrative, right-sided or multiple lesions)
Young age or a positive family history raising the possibility of Carney complex
reference.prognosis: The outlook after complete surgical excision is excellent, with low operative mortality and durable symptom relief. Recurrence of sporadic tumours is rare, but familial and Carney-complex cases recur more frequently and warrant long-term echocardiographic surveillance.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as rheumatic mitral stenosis or as infective endocarditis.
Attributing constitutional symptoms to occult malignancy or connective tissue disease while overlooking the tumour.
Omitting echocardiography in the investigation of embolic stroke of undetermined source.
Failing to screen for Carney complex in young patients or in multiple or recurrent cases.
Assuming every cardiac mass is benign and missing a rare malignant tumour.
management: Definitive treatment is prompt surgical excision of the tumour together with its base of attachment on cardiopulmonary bypass
Expedite surgery given the ongoing risk of valvular obstruction and systemic embolisation while awaiting operation
Manage obstructive heart failure and positional symptoms supportively pending resection
Address embolic complications such as cerebral or peripheral ischaemia as they arise, including embolectomy where indicated
Undertake histopathological confirmation of the resected mass or embolectomy specimen
Perform long-term echocardiographic surveillance for recurrence, especially in familial and Carney-complex disease
Screen for Carney complex and offer genetic counselling and family screening when features suggest a heritable syndrome
